blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define a movement along a production possibility curve and link the movement to the opportunity cost it carries.

blocks.heading: Sliding, not moving the boundary
blocks.text: A movement along a PPC is a reallocation of resources between the two goods while the economy stays on the boundary: more of one good, less of the other, with the maximum possible output unchanged. Sliding toward the fish axis raises fish and lowers maize. Portugal shifting workers and presses from cork plantations into machine works slides along its PPC: the capacity to do either stays as it was, and the choice changes.

blocks.heading: The cost of the slide, in figures
blocks.text: An economy's boundary runs from 60 tonnes of maize to 30 tonnes of fish. From A, 45 tonnes of maize and 15 tonnes of fish, it slides to B, 25 tonnes of maize and 25 tonnes of fish: 25 - 15 = 10 tonnes of fish gained and 45 - 25 = 20 tonnes of maize given up, 2 tonnes of maize for each tonne of fish. A further slide to C, 10 tonnes of maize and 28 tonnes of fish, gains 28 - 25 = 3 tonnes of fish for a sacrifice of 25 - 10 = 15 tonnes of maize, 5 tonnes of maize for each tonne of fish. The cost per tonne rises as the slide continues, because the resources best suited to fishing moved first and the least suited last.

blocks.heading: Movement or shift?
blocks.text: Two ideas are often run together: sliding along the boundary, and moving the boundary itself. In a movement along the PPC the economy keeps the same curve and swaps one good for the other; in a shift the whole curve relocates and the maximum possible output changes. The test is to ask what happened to the economy's capacity rather than its choice: an unchanged maximum means a movement along the curve; a maximum that has risen or fallen means the curve itself shifted.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The sacrifice measured on the slide is the opportunity cost of topic 1.3; what moves the whole boundary, and with it what the economy can produce, is the next section.
